body.text: “Modern slavery” has long been framed as a human rights violation. The extent to which it also constitutes crime is harder to talk about.
Regulatory regimes governing responsible business conduct are leaning towards mandatory human rights due diligence efforts to require action and accountability beyond mere reporting.

The United Kingdom has recently announced that it will legislate for big businesses to not only report human rights and labour exploitation risks within their operations and supply chains, but also to address those risks. This effort to align with international standards in the OECD Guidelines for Responsible Business Conduct and the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights is one that Australia’s Anti-Slavery Commissioner Chris Evans has also welcomed.

Australia has a chance to lift its modern slavery regime to meet international standards with proposals to establish a criminal offence of “failing to prevent” modern slavery in its operations and supply chain. The framework the Anti-Slavery Commissioner proposed in October advocates a “carefully designed criminal offence” that applies to the most serious criminal conduct, as a component of a broader framework response alongside a due diligence obligation.

In a recent report, New South Wales Anti-Slavery Commissioner James Cockayne alleged links between labour hire practices and organised criminal groups involved in the trade of illicit tobacco and trafficking humans for the purpose of sexual exploitation. The findings follow the NSW government’s response to 31 recommendations made by the Modern Slavery Committee on the risks faced by temporary migrant workers in regional NSW, which makes no reference to organised crime. Cockayne points to “the lack of effective, proactive policing” as a central deficiency of Australia’s response to modern slavery.

Proactive, intelligence-led policing against modern slavery – which includes human trafficking and other crimes – is the only approach that can meaningfully disrupt criminal operations. Responding to isolated incidents of human exploitation cannot identify linkages between different forms of organised crime occurring globally in which criminals do not participate in one crime type but several.

The shortcomings of reactive policing have become painfully apparent in recent manifestations of slavery. Hundreds of thousands of people have been trafficked into the global cyber-scam industry in Southeast Asia and beyond, forced – sometimes even tortured – to commit crime. Some companies implicated may be ignorant of the exploitation occurring in their supply chains, but others have been established for that purpose, providing financial and logistic support to a trillion-dollar scam economy alongside licit activities. As police scramble to keep up, the “whack-a-mole” metaphor has become hackneyed – making the point that only proactive efforts can hope to get ahead of the diffusion of criminality.

The UN reports that trafficking in persons is no longer limited to traditional forms, but that digital technologies have transformed methods of recruitment, control and exploitation. To situate modern slavery in this context, supply chains no longer comprise raw materials, manufacturers, distributors, retailers and consumers, but also social media platforms, crypto-companies, AdTech, artificial intelligence (AI) and other emerging technology companies whose business models are opaque by design.

Confronting the human rights abuses and the serious, organised crimes that occur along those chains is not the work of a regulatory regime in a country, but of several regimes across several countries, ideally working in tandem.
